analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Euclidean foreshortening shrinks by a cosine and is undone by turning the object; in Minkowski space the 'angle' is hyperbolic, the factor is 1/cosh of the rapidity, and the slice that is physically longest (the rest frame's) is not the one that looks longest on paper, so page-based visual intuition misleads. The analogy is suggestive only.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: 3D spacetime 'loaf' of a rod's world-sheet sliced by simultaneity planes of different frames.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Cosmic-ray particles that should have decayed are described as staying young by virtue of their speed, turning a lifetime calculation into a vivid ageing image.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Nothing happens to the particle internally; in its own frame the atmosphere is contracted instead.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Dual-frame animation of a muon descending: Earth frame shows dilated lifetime, muon frame shows a squashed atmosphere, same survival count.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Deepening pitch of a receding siren and reddening of light
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Uses the familiar sound experience to set up the sign of the effect before computing it for light.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Sound needs a medium and has different formulae for moving source versus moving observer; for light only relative velocity matters relativistically.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Galaxies as particles on hyperbolic world-lines
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A family of uniformly accelerated particles is compared to galaxies in some cosmological models, anticipating horizons in cosmology.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Real cosmological horizons arise from expansion in curved spacetime, not from acceleration in flat spacetime; the analogy is flagged only as a preview of Chapter 25.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Negative spatial terms in the metric as a reversed Pythagoras
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Moving in space subtracts from the spacetime length, so the bent path that looks longer on paper has less proper time; a reversed triangle inequality.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The diagram is still drawn with Euclidean eyes, so the intuition must be retrained rather than transferred.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Path-length comparison tool: learner draws two paths between the same events and sees Euclidean length and proper time ranked oppositely.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A boost is just an ordinary rotation of the (x, ct) axes.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A boost is a hyperbolic rotation: both axes tilt towards the light line by arctan(v/c), and scales along them change; only the hyperbolae are preserved.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The cos/sin to cosh/sinh analogy and the word 'rotation' invite a rigid picture.
concepts: spacetime diagram of two inertial observers

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Length contraction is a physical squashing of the object caused by motion through a medium, so one frame sees the 'real' contraction.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The relativistic effect requires no ether, is reciprocal between frames, and follows from different simultaneity slices of the same world-tube.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Historically FitzGerald and Lorentz proposed exactly such a dynamical mechanism, and everyday contraction always involves forces.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Moving objects are also shrunk perpendicular to their motion.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Dimensions transverse to the relative velocity are unchanged (y' = y, z' = z).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Learners generalize 'moving things shrink' to all directions.
concepts: spatial isotropy argument for transverse coordinates

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since y' = y, the transverse velocity components are unchanged by a boost along x.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Transverse velocities change by 1/[beta(1 - u1 v/c^2)] because the frames measure different time intervals.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Galilean intuition and the unchanged transverse coordinates.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The skewed S' axes on S's diagram have the same tick spacing as S's axes.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Units along ct' and x' must be found from the invariant hyperbolae; on paper they are longer by ((1 + v^2/c^2)/(1 - v^2/c^2))^{1/2}.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Diagrams look Euclidean and learners measure with a ruler.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If each inertial observer sees the other's clock run slow, the twins' situation is symmetric and neither can be younger.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The traveller changes inertial frame; the two world-lines between departure and reunion are different, and the inertial one has the greater proper time.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Reciprocity of time dilation is emphasized just before, and the accelerations can be made brief.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Acceleration itself slows the travelling twin's clock, so the age difference is created during the turnaround.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: By the clock hypothesis acceleration does not affect an ideal clock's rate; the deficit accumulates along the whole path, and making the turnaround shorter does not remove it. What the turnaround changes is the traveller's simultaneity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book stresses that brief accelerations have finite effects, which can be misread as the clocks being affected.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The world-line that looks longer on a spacetime diagram has more elapsed time.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Spatial displacement enters ds^2 with a minus sign, so the bent path has less proper time than the straight one.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Euclidean habit of reading lengths off paper.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Uniform acceleration in relativity means dv/dt constant in a fixed inertial frame.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Relativistic uniform acceleration is constant acceleration in the momentary rest frame; the lab-frame dv/dt decreases as (1 - u^2/c^2)^{3/2}.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is the Newtonian definition and the simplest reading of the words.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Acceleration is relative in special relativity just as velocity is.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: All inertial observers agree whether a body accelerates; only the numerical components differ. Acceleration becomes relative only in general relativity (in the sense of free fall counting as unaccelerated).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The theory is called relativity and velocity is relative, so learners extend it.
concepts: absoluteness of acceleration in special relativity

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A Doppler shift requires motion towards or away from the observer.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A source with zero radial velocity but non-zero speed still shows a redshift by beta, the transverse Doppler effect, due to time dilation.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Classically and for sound the shift depends only on the radial component.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Special relativity is only needed for accelerated objects; accelerations take you outside special relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Special relativity handles accelerated motion perfectly well in flat spacetime, as the chapter's proper-time integral and hyperbolic motion show; general relativity is needed for gravity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The twin paradox is often 'resolved' by saying acceleration requires general relativity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Time dilation means the moving clock merely looks slow because its light takes time to arrive.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: T = beta T0 compares coordinate times after light delays are removed; what one actually sees also includes the Doppler factor, which can be a blueshift for approach.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Seeing and measuring are conflated; the Doppler section combines both effects.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Perpendicular lines in one inertial frame are perpendicular in every frame, so 'parallel frames' is an obvious notion.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A rod at a given angle in its rest frame has a different angle in another frame, so axes need not look rectangular to the other observer; 'parallel' needs careful definition.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Rotations and translations preserve angles, and Galilean intuition extends that to boosts.

thought_experiments.name: Light flash from coincident origins
thought_experiments.setup: At the instant the origins of S and S' coincide, a flash is emitted; each observer describes the expanding front.
thought_experiments.lesson: Both must see a sphere centred on their own origin expanding at c, which forces the interval to be preserved.
concepts: constancy of the speed of light
thought_experiments.app_idea: 3D light-cone viewer: one expanding sphere drawn in two frames' simultaneity slices, each appearing centred on its own origin.

thought_experiments.name: Measuring a moving rod
thought_experiments.setup: A rod rests in S'; S records where its ends are at one S-time.
thought_experiments.lesson: Length depends on the frame's simultaneity; the moving rod is shorter by beta.

thought_experiments.name: Ticks of a moving clock
thought_experiments.setup: A clock fixed at one position in S' ticks twice; S records the times of these ticks.
thought_experiments.lesson: Proper interval is shortest; other inertial observers assign beta times more.

thought_experiments.name: Rocket with constant exhaust rate
thought_experiments.setup: A spaceship's motor runs at a steady rate so the crew feels constant acceleration.
thought_experiments.lesson: Its Earth-frame world-line is a hyperbola; speed approaches c asymptotically and some light signals sent after it can never catch up.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Cockpit view plus Earth-frame diagram, with light pulses launched from Earth at chosen times; late pulses visibly never reach the rocket.

thought_experiments.name: Hyperbolically moving swarm of particles
thought_experiments.setup: A system of particles each on a hyperbola centred at O, filling two opposite wedges bounded by light rays.
thought_experiments.lesson: Light at 45 degrees cannot cross between wedges, so the light rays act as event horizons.

thought_experiments.name: Twin paradox
thought_experiments.setup: Twin A-bar accelerates away, cruises, reverses at a star and returns; twin A stays on Earth.
thought_experiments.lesson: Only the traveller changes frames; the traveller's simultaneity swings at turnaround and the bent world-line has less proper time, so the traveller is younger.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Dual clock race with an adjustable journey and a live 'what is home doing now' readout from the traveller's simultaneity line.

thought_experiments.name: Source circling the observer
thought_experiments.setup: A light source moves in a circle about the origin of S at constant speed, so it never approaches or recedes.
thought_experiments.lesson: A redshift by beta still appears: transverse Doppler shift as a clean signature of time dilation.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Rotor animation with a central detector and a spectral line shifting as rotor speed increases.

thought_experiments.name: Athlete with a pole in a short room (Exercise 3.6)
thought_experiments.setup: An athlete carrying an 8 m pole at beta = 2 runs into a 4 m room and shuts the door.
thought_experiments.lesson: In the room frame the pole fits; in the athlete frame the room is 2 m, and the resolution rests on no signal outrunning light, so the pole's far end cannot stop instantly.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Split-screen spacetime diagrams in room and pole frames with door events and stopping signal fronts.

thought_experiments.name: Running a red light (Exercise 3.12)
thought_experiments.setup: A driver approaches a red traffic light fast enough that it looks green.
thought_experiments.lesson: Radial Doppler shift inverts to the required speed, a sizeable fraction of c.

historical_notes.event: FitzGerald proposed that bodies moving through the ether shorten along their motion, possibly via electrical intermolecular forces, to explain the Michelson-Morley null result; Lorentz and Poincare elaborated it by modifying electromagnetic forces; Einstein reinterpreted the contraction kinematically without an ether.
historical_notes.significance: Illustrates the shift from an ad hoc dynamical hypothesis in an absolute frame to a reciprocal consequence of the relativity of simultaneity.

historical_notes.event: Some opponents of special relativity built counter-arguments on the false assumption that a boost acts as an ordinary rotation of the (x, ct) plane.
historical_notes.significance: Shows why the hyperbolic character of boosts matters in practice.

historical_notes.event: The twin (clock) paradox was the subject of a controversy that flared repeatedly over more than fifty years.
historical_notes.significance: Motivates careful treatment of acceleration, simultaneity and route dependence of time.

historical_notes.event: Atomic clocks flown around the world were compared with a ground clock and found to have lost the relativistically predicted amount.
historical_notes.significance: Direct test of time dilation with macroscopic clocks (identified by us as the 1971 Hafele-Keating experiment; the book gives no names or date).

historical_notes.event: Mossbauer-effect experiments with rotating apparatus confirmed the transverse Doppler shift.
historical_notes.significance: Verified time dilation through a purely relativistic spectral shift (the early rotor experiments date from around 1960; dates are our addition).

applications_and_observations.details: Clocks carried round the world on aircraft compared with a ground clock; the book reports agreement with relativity for the travelling clock's lag.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Book gives no numbers. Our addition: Hafele-Keating (1971) measured roughly -59 ns eastward and +273 ns westward, including gravitational and Earth-rotation effects.

applications_and_observations.details: Short-lived particles made at the top of the atmosphere survive to the ground only because their lifetimes are dilated in the Earth frame.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Book: without dilation the travel time would exceed the proper lifetime by factors of order 10. Our estimate: muon proper lifetime about 2.2 microseconds, c tau about 660 m, production altitude about 10-15 km.

applications_and_observations.topic: Transverse Doppler shift with Mossbauer rotors
applications_and_observations.details: Rotating source/absorber arrangements detect the second-order shift predicted by (3.27).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Shift fraction about v^2/(2c^2); for rim speeds of a few hundred m/s this is of order 10^-12 (our estimate), accessible only with Mossbauer line widths.

applications_and_observations.details: Cruise speed chosen so that the Lorentz factor is 2, halving the Earth-star distance in the traveller's frame.

applications_and_observations.topic: Hyperbolic motions and horizons in cosmology
applications_and_observations.details: Families of uniformly accelerated world-lines with horizons are previewed as relevant to cosmological models, with galaxies as the particles.
Small-time expansion tau approximately T(1 - alpha^2T^2/(6c^2)) applied to a 3g rocket.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimates: after 1 hour the ship clock lags by about 75 microseconds; after 10 days by about 17 minutes (alpha T/c about 0.085).

applications_and_observations.details: Constant 1 g acceleration in years and light-years (g about 1.03 ly/yr^2) for long proper times.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimates: 22 years of proper time covers about 3 x 10^9 light-years; four 6-year legs (accelerate, decelerate, accelerate back, decelerate) correspond to roughly 940 years on Earth.

applications_and_observations.details: Approach speed needed to blueshift 700 nm to 500 nm using the radial Doppler formula.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimate: (1 - v/c)/(1 + v/c) = 25/49 gives v = 12c/37, about 0.32c or 1 x 10^8 m/s.

applications_and_observations.details: Minimum room length for the pole trick with an 8 m pole at beta = 2.

notation_and_conventions.convention: beta(v) denotes the Lorentz factor (1 - v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}, defined with := .

notation_and_conventions.convention: The chapter uses non-relativistic units with c explicit, but switches to relativistic units c = 1 for the hyperbolic-rotation derivation and when comparing with Chapter 2.

notation_and_conventions.convention: v is the relative speed of the frames; u = (u1, u2, u3) is a particle's velocity in S, primes for S'; u_r is a source's radial velocity.
Unprimed quantities refer to S, primed to S'; S' moves along the positive x-axis of S with origins coinciding at t = t' = 0.

A is the stay-at-home twin; A-bar (A with an overbar) is the traveller.
k denotes the radial Doppler (Bondi) factor from Chapter 2.
Key results such as (3.24)-(3.27) are printed in shaded boxes; new terms are set in bold.

margin_notes.summary: Parenthetical warning that some past critics of relativity mistook a boost for a genuine rotation of the (x, ct) plane and built faulty objections on it.

In-text aside: the authors concede that nobody has settled experimentally whether human ageing slows with speed, but argue that bodies are built from atoms, and atoms are seen to obey time dilation, so people should too.
Caveat that deciding what physically counts as a clock or an ideal clock is not a trivial question.
Instruction to compare the rapidity-derived composition law with equation (2.6) of Chapter 2.
Pointer that hyperbolic motions matter in cosmology (Chapter 25) and that event horizons will be important later.
Remark that, unlike in special relativity, acceleration will not be absolute in general relativity.
The radial Doppler figure is described as a merger of Fig. 2.7 (k-calculus radar) with Fig. 3.12.
Exercise 3.6 hint suggests looking up discussions of the pole-in-the-barn paradox online.
Further reading recommends Rindler's Introduction to Special Relativity (1982) and Marder's An Introduction to Relativity (1968), the latter by a former Southampton colleague.

difficulty.notes: Algebra is elementary (differentials, hyperbolic identities, one separable ODE), but the chapter moves quickly and relies on Chapter 2 for the isotropy argument and interpretation. Conceptual load peaks in §3.6 (reading skewed, rescaled axes), §3.8 (horizons stated without proof) and §3.9 (twin paradox resolution is compact and its numerical sketch is loosely worded). Several printing slips on p.39 (arctan written as tan, swapped coordinate ratios, an unlabelled point E) can trip careful readers. Exercises 3.3, 3.6 and 3.9 are noticeably harder than the text.

teaching_gems.gem: Treat the boost as a hyperbolic rotation so rapidity adds; the relativistic velocity law then falls out of the tanh addition formula.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Replaces an unmotivated algebraic formula with a familiar structure (rotation angles add) and explains at once why speeds never exceed c (tanh is bounded).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Rapidity number line: learner stacks boost 'arrows' end to end on an unbounded rapidity axis while a tanh-mapped velocity axis below compresses them into (-c, c).

teaching_gems.gem: Draw the invariant hyperbolae once and let them calibrate every frame's units on the same diagram.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Removes the biggest trap of Minkowski diagrams (reading scale off paper) and makes reciprocity of contraction and dilation visible without algebra.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Multi-frame calibrated diagram where axes of any number of frames snap their tick marks to fixed hyperbolae.

teaching_gems.gem: Before subtracting transformed coordinates, name the two events and the frame in which they are simultaneous or co-located.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns contraction and dilation into a single protocol and inoculates against sign and reciprocity confusions.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Event-picking exercise: learner must click the two events to be compared before any formula appears; wrong choices show what quantity they actually computed.

teaching_gems.gem: Show the travelling twin's simultaneity lines before and after turnaround, leaving an uncovered stretch of the home twin's world-line.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes the asymmetry concrete and geometric, and explains where 'missing' home time goes without invoking forces on clocks.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Animated sweeping 'now' line tied to the traveller with a plot of assigned home time versus traveller proper time showing the jump.

teaching_gems.gem: Define uniform acceleration in the momentary rest frame and integrate to a hyperbola, then use 45-degree light rays to discover horizons in flat spacetime.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Introduces horizons, a central general relativity idea, with no curvature and only elementary calculus.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Chase-the-rocket game: learner times light pulses from Earth to catch an accelerating rocket and finds a cutoff time beyond which no pulse arrives.

teaching_gems.gem: Build the relativistic Doppler formula as the classical pulse-delay argument times one time-dilation factor, then split into radial and transverse cases.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Separates two physical effects cleanly, links back to the k-factor, and isolates the transverse shift as a direct test of time dilation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Doppler decomposer with stacked bars for 'extra travel time' and 'dilated emission', plus angle control from head-on to transverse.

teaching_gems.gem: Compare what is absolute in Newtonian theory, special relativity and general relativity in a single table.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives a memorable map of the conceptual progression and a hook for why general relativity is needed.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Interactive absolute/relative sorting table with per-cell demonstrations.

teaching_gems.gem: Explain why the bent world-line is longer on paper yet records less time via the minus signs in the metric.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Directly confronts Euclidean diagram intuition with the reversed triangle inequality.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Two-path comparison tool listing Euclidean length and proper time side by side as the learner reshapes a path.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Property 1 on p.39 says the axes skew inwards through the angle tan(v/c); the correct angle is arctan(v/c) (the x'-axis has slope v/c).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A careful reader computing the tilt gets a wrong angle or doubts the diagram.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the tilt as arctan(v/c) and show slope v/c directly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The reading rule for S' coordinates is printed as (ct', x') = (OU/OA, OV/OB), which swaps components relative to the book's own (ct', x') = (OV, OU); it should be (OV/OB, OU/OA).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners following the formula assign distances to times and vice versa.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the corrected order and label which axis each point lies on.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Property 3 refers to a segment OE, but no point E is labelled in Fig. 3.7; the intended unit segment on the x'-axis is OA.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers search the figure for E and lose the reciprocity argument.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Replace OE by OA or label the point.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In §3.9 the speed is typeset as a square root over 3c divided by 2 (meaning (sqrt(3)/2)c), and the sentence 'from A's viewpoint ... A-bar finds' mixes the two twins' perspectives.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The beta = 2 estimate is hard to reproduce and the frame in which the distance is halved is unclear.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write v = (sqrt(3)/2)c, compute beta = 2 explicitly, and say that in the traveller's cruise frame the Earth-star distance is halved.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The step from I = 0 iff I' = 0 plus linearity to I = nI' is asserted; it needs the lemma that two quadratic forms with the same (Lorentzian) null cone are proportional. Likewise the hyperbolic-rotation form (3.7)-(3.8) is adopted by analogy rather than derived, silently excluding reflections.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Mathematically minded readers may feel the derivation is circular or incomplete.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short proof for 1+1 dimensions (compare coefficients of the null directions) and note the orthochronous, parity-preserving choice.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Linearity is motivated by straight lines mapping to straight lines, but projective (fractional-linear) maps also do this; homogeneity of space and time is the missing assumption.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The derivation looks more airtight than it is.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Name homogeneity of spacetime as the extra assumption, or quote the fundamental theorem of affine geometry: a bijection of the whole of R^4 that sends every line to a line is affine.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The symbol beta is used for the Lorentz factor, whereas most other sources use gamma, and alpha is overloaded (rapidity, v/c in Exercise 3.2, acceleration in Exercise 3.9).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion when learners consult other books or online material.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Keep a notation crosswalk visible (beta_DIV = gamma elsewhere) and rename overloaded symbols in the app.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Table 3.1 lists acceleration as relative in general relativity without qualification.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think accelerometer readings become frame-dependent; in fact proper acceleration is invariant, and what changes is that free fall counts as unaccelerated.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Distinguish proper (felt) acceleration from coordinate acceleration when presenting the table; point to the equivalence principle.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The statement that acceleration is not a vector in Minkowski space refers to the 3-acceleration components; the four-acceleration is a genuine four-vector, introduced later.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may conclude acceleration has no covariant description.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say 'the three-acceleration is not the spatial part of a four-vector' and forward-link to the four-acceleration in Chapter 8.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The flown-clock experiment is described as matching relativity precisely, without noting that gravitational time dilation and the Earth's rotation (east versus west flights) are essential, and the ground clock is not inertial.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Oversimplified evidence may be challenged by informed learners.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present the Hafele-Keating numbers with their kinematic and gravitational parts.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Dated wording: the cosmic-ray particles are called mesons (they are muons, leptons), and biological ageing under time dilation is called an open question.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may repeat outdated terminology or think time dilation might spare living things.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use 'muons' and state that all physical processes, including biological ones, are subject to time dilation.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The constancy of radar distance between hyperbolic motions and the horizon claim are stated without proof or computation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers must take a non-obvious result on trust; the family chosen (common centre, different a) matters.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide the one-line radar calculation for Rindler observers, or use Exercise 3.9 to show the horizon explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In (3.25) u_r is the radial velocity in S while v is the full speed, and the classical derivation implicitly treats S as a preferred rest frame; the transverse case also depends on in which frame the motion is perpendicular to the line of sight.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners mix u_r with v, and may get a blueshift for 'transverse' when the angle is defined in the source frame.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Define the angle explicitly in the observer's frame at reception, and show the circular-orbit case where the ambiguity vanishes.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 3.3 marks the proper interval T0 as a vertical bracket beside the clock's world-line, not along it, so the drawing does not distinguish T0 from a coordinate-time separation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Novices may read T0 as shorter vertical height rather than as a proper time along a tilted line.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Place T0 along the world-line and calibrate with a hyperbola in the redesign.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The twin resolution says the accelerations have immediate finite effects, which can be misread as acceleration slowing clocks, conflicting with the clock hypothesis stated in §3.4.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners attribute the age gap to the turnaround forces.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Emphasize that the gap accumulates along the cruise legs and that acceleration only changes the traveller's simultaneity; show that shortening the turnaround leaves the gap.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In Exercise 3.11 the received frequency is printed with a symbol resembling v rather than nu.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confuses frequency with speed in formulae that already contain u and c.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'In Chapter 2 we got the Lorentz transformation from radar and the k-factor. Can you think of another route that uses only the light flash and the relativity principle?' Then walk through the light-sphere argument.

Bridge from rotations: ask the learner what quantity a rotation preserves and what formula it has, then ask what should change if the preserved quantity is x^2 - t^2. Let them guess cosh and sinh before revealing (3.7)-(3.8).

Before every contraction or dilation calculation, make the learner name the two events and the frame in which they are simultaneous or co-located. Check: 'Which events did you compare, and whose clock or ruler recorded them?'

Check reciprocity understanding: 'S says S' clocks run slow; S' says S clocks run slow. Why is this not a contradiction?' Expected answer involves different pairs of events and relativity of simultaneity.
Watch for beta/gamma confusion when learners have used other resources; say explicitly that this book's beta is gamma elsewhere.
When drawing S' axes, ask for the slopes first (v/c and c/v), then ask 'is one tick on ct' the same length on paper as one tick on ct?' and use the hyperbolae to settle it.
For acceleration, ask: 'If a particle has zero acceleration in S, can it accelerate in S'?' Use (3.20)-(3.22) to answer no, then preview how general relativity changes this with free fall.

Uniform acceleration: ask why constant dv/dt fails, then have the learner compute the speed after a very long time from u(t) to see it approach c. Ask where light sent from the origin after t = c/a goes.

Twin paradox order: (1) state the symmetric-sounding argument, (2) ask what distinguishes the twins, (3) show simultaneity lines jumping, (4) compute proper times, (5) relate to the minus sign in ds^2. Probe the misconception that acceleration slows clocks.
Doppler check: 'A source moves in a circle around you. Classically, is there a shift? Relativistically?' Then ask how this tests time dilation independently of light-travel effects.

Common learner questions: Why is length contraction not seen in photographs (Terrell-Penrose rotation, beyond the chapter)? Does the travelling twin feel time slow down (no, local physics is unchanged)? Is rapidity physical (yes, it is what an on-board accelerometer integrates for straight-line motion: rapidity = a tau/c).
Flag the p.39 slips proactively when a learner reads the book: arctan(v/c), the swapped (ct', x') ratios, and OE meaning OA.
For advanced learners, extend to non-collinear boosts via Exercise 3.3 and mention that two non-parallel boosts compose to a boost plus rotation (Thomas-Wigner), which the chapter does not cover.
